title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
extended_summary:
This paper examines the rapid emergence of generative AI chatbots—especially ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie—and considers their implications for higher education. The authors aim to situate these tools historically and commercially, review early English- and Chinese-language academic literature, and compare leading chatbots on capabilities relevant to higher education assessment, teaching, and learning. A central concern is how these systems may disrupt traditional academic practices, especially writing-based assessment and academic integrity.

The paper does not report a participant-based intervention study. Instead, it combines historical overview, literature review, and comparative analysis of chatbot systems. The authors describe the development of chatbots from ELIZA to current large language model systems, discuss the role of major US and Chinese technology firms, and review early scholarly discussions on chatbot use in higher education. They also outline a comparative testing approach to assess chatbot performance on tasks relevant to academic assignments and examinations.

The context is higher education rather than K-12 schooling. The discussion concerns students, faculty, and institutions broadly, with examples drawn from university assessment, learning support, and disciplinary applications such as medicine, law, IT security, and language learning. The article also references institutional and policy responses, including bans, revised assessments, and concerns about plagiarism detection.

The paper concludes that, despite substantial hype, current chatbots are far from consistently reliable or truly intelligent. GPT-4 and earlier ChatGPT models performed best among the systems discussed, while Bing Chat and Bard were characterized as less dependable in the authors’ comparison. The authors argue that higher education should neither ignore nor simply ban these tools; instead, institutions, faculty, and students should respond critically and adapt assessment and teaching practices to the new generative AI landscape.
quality_tier_rationale: Although published in a peer-reviewed journal, this paper is primarily a narrative review and comparative commentary focused on higher education, without a clear K-12 empirical design, student sample, or causal methodology aligned to the requested evidence framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important but unclear institutional and productivity implications of chatbot adoption; however, it does not report direct learner impact estimates or effect sizes, so impact remains speculative and unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Comparative review and benchmark-style evaluation of general-purpose generative AI chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, GPT-4, Bing Chat, Bard, Ernie) for higher-education-relevant tasks such as answering questions, generating text, providing explanations, and supporting academic work.

finding.finding_summary: This article argues that rapidly developing chatbot systems are likely to substantially affect higher education assessment, teaching, learning, and institutional policy, but it does not present original causal evidence from learners or schools. Its own comparative bot test concluded that no chatbot in the sampled cohort achieved top-tier performance, with GPT-4 performing best and Bing Chat/Bard performing poorly on the authors' higher-education-relevant benchmark; however, no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or student outcome statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Comparative author-designed chatbot performance test and narrative review of implications for higher education policy, assessment, and teaching

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses potential productivity gains from generative AI for drafting, editing, summarising, and producing materials, while simultaneously emphasizing unreliability, hallucinations, and accuracy problems that limit safe educational use. These claims are based on literature review and illustrative examples rather than an empirical study of teacher or student efficiency outcomes, and no quantitative workload or time-savings estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of productivity/workload affordances and risks of chatbot use in academic tasks
